text.markdown:
*Community server-farm & deep-net dive*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Cold Stack announces itself before you see it — a bass-deep exhale of chilled air rolling out between two shanty-towers, and under it, a hum that isn't quite sound, more a pressure behind your back teeth. When the alley opens up you understand why: a server-farm the size of a cathedral, forty stories of scavenged rack-cabinets welded into the tower's dead structural bones, wrapped floor to ceiling in cable like ivy grown feral. There is no sky above it — only the black gasket-seams of the level overhead, sweating that warm chemical rain down onto the stack's roof in fat, hissing drops that flash to steam a foot from the hottest vents.

Between you and the Stack, the district's traffic sorts itself into a strange, layered ballet. Courier-drones hug the ceiling-dark in blinking lines, threading around a Meridian relay-gantry strung with a hundred jury-rigged antennae. A cargo-crawler grinds past at knee height, dragging a sled of coolant drums, forcing pedestrians up onto cable-spool sidewalks that sway underfoot. Somewhere close a hovercab noses down out of the murk, running lights smeared to long pink-and-cyan streaks in the standing rain, and lands nowhere in particular because there is nowhere in particular to land. Every wall here glows — not with ads, but with the Stack's own status-runes, cyan data-conduit lines pulsing along the gutters like exposed veins, carrying the district's lifeblood of bandwidth out to a thousand shanty-hab feeds.

Up close, the cooling-mist rolling off the Stack's louvers beads on your jacket and tastes of ozone and machine oil. Somewhere inside that wall of humming metal, a hundred people are sleeping, dreaming, working, or dying wired into something that isn't quite a place.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Auntie Ferro** — a Corran guild-clan elder who "owns" the Stack the way a shepherd owns a flock: she doesn't control it, she tends it, brokering rack-space, settling disputes, and feeding anyone who keeps the cooling fans running. Everyone in Wireside owes her a favor or fears losing one.

**Deckhand Priya** — a self-taught Technomancer barely out of her teens who lives inside the Stack's crawlspaces, running diagnostics in exchange for a cot and deep-net access. She hears things in the noise-floor no one else does.

**Warden Oyelaran** — Ferrum's nominal landlord-rep, a tired mid-boss who collects "structural tax" and otherwise leaves the Stack alone because shutting it down would black out half the district.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — community-held. Auntie Ferro's informal authority, tolerated by Ferrum as long as the tax gets paid.

No standing guard, but the Stack is watched constantly — a hundred residents with a stake in it. Theft or sabotage draws a fast, physical, and collective response, not corp Alert. Ferrum sends an enforcer crew only if the tax stops; they come loud, in a cargo-rig, and leave once paid or once someone bleeds.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Cold Stack is one of the brightest nodes in Wireside's data-map — a visible knot of traffic any hacker's overlay will flag on sight. Public AR shows only maintenance schematics and Ferro's barter-board; the real traffic (deep-net relays, black-market bandwidth resale, three dead-drops in the coolant-duct access panels) sits one layer down, guarded by Priya's homebrew ICE.

Technomancers describe the Stack's noise-floor as "haunted" — ghost-packets that don't resolve to any known protocol, looping in the deep architecture. Most call it corrupted legacy code. Priya isn't so sure.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Ferro's Favor. Auntie Ferro calls in an old debt: someone is skimming rack-space contracts to funnel bandwidth to an unknown buyer uptower. She wants the crew to find out who — and whether Meridian is already watching.

2. The Noise-Floor. Priya has isolated a recurring ghost-signal that resembles a corrupted Technomancer's sending — impossible, since the last known Stack diver of that skill died six years ago. The signal is getting louder, and it's asking for help.

3. Structural Tax. Ferrum quietly triples the Stack's tax, timed to a citywide "infrastructure audit" tied to the war effort above. If the crew can't find leverage fast, Auntie Ferro's people go dark — literally and financially.

text.markdown:
*Bandwidth & rig-parts black market*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The street here doesn't so much have a ceiling as a lid — the sagging underbelly of the district above, patched in places with corrugate sheeting where the original structure gave out decades ago, dripping its endless warm rain into gutters that hiss and steam. Cable Souk fills the gap beneath it wall to wall: stall after stall of salvaged spool-wire, bootleg decks, cracked optics, and coils of fiber sold by the meter off spindles taller than a man, every table lit by its own cheap sign bleeding sodium-gold and cyan into the wet.

Overhead, in the narrow slot of open air the souk's canopies leave clear, the traffic never stops — courier-drones weaving single-file above the stalls, a hovercab drifting sideways to avoid a low gantry, and below them all a line of ground-rigs crawling bumper to bumper, horns and hawkers' cries fighting for the same air. The noise is layered like the traffic: engine-whine under vendor-chant under the wet slap of tarps under, always, that deep foundation heartbeat thrumming up through the souk's cracked pavement.

You feel the souk clock you before you've taken ten steps in — a dozen vendors' eyes flicking to your rig, your chrome, the cut of your jacket, doing the math on what you're worth to rob, to sell to, or to warn away.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Broker Yuen** — runs the souk's unofficial exchange rate for bandwidth futures; a Nyx-adjacent fixer who trades favors as often as scrip and remembers every debt down to the decimal.

**Big Marsh** — a hulking ex-Ironclad quartermaster turned rig-parts dealer, selling combat-frame components that "fell off a convoy." Everyone knows better than to ask which convoy.

**The Twins** — two identical, unnervingly quiet vendors who deal exclusively in grey-tech decks and never give the same name twice; rumored Cinderhold couriers laundering gear through the souk.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — lawless-by-consensus. No single gang rules it; the vendors police each other because a riot is bad for everyone's business.

Petty theft gets mob justice on the spot. Anything bigger — a shootout, a corp raid — scatters the souk in seconds, stalls folding into mobile carts and vanishing down side-alleys within a minute. Alert here means the souk simply isn't there anymore.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Public AR is a chaotic flea-market of floating price-tags, fake reviews, and vendor reputation scores, half of them gamed. Underneath, the souk runs a private barter-ledger on a pirate mesh-net that never touches the corp backbone — a hacker who finds the mesh finds an unregulated, untaxed economy worth a fortune to expose or exploit.

Meridian's official coverage of the souk is thin by design — a "dead patch" bought and maintained by pooled vendor bribes, one of the few blind spots in the Wired this far down.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Grey Market Audit. A batch of "fallen off a convoy" combat-frame parts from Big Marsh turns out to be tagged Ironclad war matériel headed for the front. Someone up the chain wants it back quietly — or wants the leak found loudly.

2. The Twins' Ledger. The Twins go missing along with their entire stock, and their mesh-net dead-drop starts broadcasting a garbled distress loop. Cinderhold wants the crew to find out if it's a corp snatch or something in the deep-net that got out.

3. Blind Patch. Someone is buying up the souk's Meridian bribe-fund from the outside, threatening to flood the blind spot with surveillance. The vendors need muscle, money, or a miracle before their dead patch goes live.

text.markdown:
*Technomancer haunt; net-runners for hire*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

There's no sign, just a hole in a cooling-tower's foundation wall where a door used to be, and a stairwell going down instead of up — which in Wireside is the closest thing to a landmark you get. Rain sheets off the tower above in ropes, catching cyan light bounced off the data-conduits running along the gutter, and by the time you've crossed the street your boots are soaked through. Above the doorway a single flickering holo-sign reads THE DIVE, half the letters dead.

The street traffic here is thinner but no less layered — a lone courier-drone parked on a ledge like a roosting bird, a boosted ground-rig idling at the curb with its Technomancer owner still half-jacked into its dash-deck, eyes rolled back, lips moving to a conversation happening somewhere else entirely. Somewhere above, unseen, an aircraft's running lights slide across the underside of the level-ceiling, gone before you can track it.

Down the stairs the air changes — cooler, drier, humming with deck-fans and old amp static. A dozen jacks are plugged into a dozen skulls at the bar, bodies slack, minds somewhere in the Wired. The bartender doesn't look up. He already knows why you're here.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Sable** — the Dive's owner-bartender, an old Technomancer who "retired" from deep-net running after something down there left half his face numb; now he brokers net-runner contracts for a cut and never explains the numbness.

**Kess Oduya** — the Dive's best working net-runner, young, arrogant, brilliant, freelance for hire to anyone who can meet her price; despises corp work but will take it if the money's obscene enough.

**The Hollow Man** — a regular who never removes his jack, speaks only in half-sentences, and is either the best diver in the district or something that used to be a person and now just wears one's face. No one's checked closely enough to be sure.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Technomancer-informal. Sable's word is law inside; outside is whatever gang controls that block that week.

Violence inside the Dive is almost unheard of — jacked-in patrons are catatonic and utterly defenseless, and everyone knows it, so an unwritten code protects them fiercely. Break it once and you're barred from every deep-net den in Wireside within a day; Technomancers talk.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

To a normal AR scan, the Dive reads as an unlicensed net-café, nothing more. To anyone jacked in, it's a doorway — Sable maintains one of the district's cleanest, fastest deep-net on-ramps, a rarity worth protecting.

Under the surface, the Dive's private board lists net-runners for hire by reputation, not name — a hacker who cracks it finds real identities, blackmail-grade information on half the district's talent.

Kess's persona in the Wired burns unusually bright — Technomancers who've crossed her signature say it doesn't feel entirely human anymore.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Hire the Diver. A client needs a net-runner for a job too hot for their usual talent. Sable will broker the introduction to Kess — for a price, and a favor owed to the house.

2. The Hollow Man's Errand. The Hollow Man surfaces from a jack-in for the first time in months, hands the crew a data-shard, and says only "finish it" before going under again. What's on the shard implicates a Meridian watch-captain in something ugly.

3. Sable's Numbness. Something from Sable's old final dive is resurfacing in the deep-net — a signature only he'd recognize. He wants the crew to escort him back in, one more time, to close a door he never properly shut.

text.markdown:
*Cooling-fog cover; deals & ambushes*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You smell Mist Alley before you see it — hot metal and coolant chemical, sweet and acrid together — and then you're in it, and the world goes soft-edged and gold. The alley runs between two cooling-tower blocks whose overflow vents dump superheated exhaust straight into the standing rain, and the collision boils up a fog that never fully clears, lit sodium-gold by a string of caged bulbs no one's bothered to steal. There is no sky here, less than anywhere — just the fog, and above the fog, somewhere, the black gasket-seam underside of the level overhead, invisible tonight behind the mist.

Shapes move through it at every height: a courier-drone's running lights smear to a soft halo as it threads overhead, a ground-rig's headlamps become two golden smudges before the vehicle itself resolves out of the murk close enough to graze your shoulder, gone again just as fast. Voices arrive before faces do. Footsteps arrive before voices. You can hear the alley's whole life happening around you — a transaction, a laugh, a scuffle — and see none of it until it's three feet away.

Everyone in Wireside knows what Mist Alley is for. Half the deals in this district happen in this fog because no camera holds a clean image here — and so does every ambush that ever needed the same cover.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Whisper Cole** — a Nyx-affiliated broker who conducts sensitive meets exclusively in the mist, trusting the fog more than any encryption; pays well for discretion and punishes its absence personally.

**Dredge** — a scavenger who works the alley's runoff grates for anything dropped, lost, or hidden in a hurry; knows the fog's blind spots better than anyone alive and sells that knowledge cheap.

**Captain Reyes** — leads a small Ironclad-contracted patrol that sweeps the alley twice a night on paper and once in reality; corruptible, exhausted, and one bad night from snapping.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — contested/no-man's cover. No faction truly holds it; everyone uses it, so everyone tacitly protects the fog's usefulness by not clearing it.

The mist defeats most visual security entirely — thermal and sonar work poorly through the coolant-vapor turbulence. Violence here escalates fast and unseen; by the time anyone reacts, it's usually already over. Ironclad's patrol responds to gunfire, not screams.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The fog is a literal blind spot in the visual-surveillance net, and Meridian's coverage maps show it as a known, tolerated dead zone — too expensive to fix, too useful to certain corp interests to actually want fixed.

AR overlays degrade badly in the mist's particulate interference; tags flicker, ghost, and sometimes show stale data hours or days old — an Edgerunner reading the alley's AR layer may be looking at a version of the street that no longer exists.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Fog Meet. Whisper Cole wants the crew as muscle for a meet gone paranoid — a Meridian defector trading data for a new SIN, and someone's already tipped off the buyer's rivals.

2. What Dredge Found. Dredge surfaces a corp ID-chip from the runoff grates, still warm, belonging to someone who was never reported missing. Following the thread means finding out who's disappearing people in the mist and why no one's looking.

3. Reyes's Breaking Point. Captain Reyes is about to snap and either flip on Ironclad or get someone innocent killed trying to prove he hasn't gone soft. The crew gets pulled into his last patrol, one way or the other.

text.markdown:
*Haunted deep-net access; dark spot*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The block around Ghost Node is too quiet, and in Wireside that's its own kind of scream. The chemical rain still falls from the level-underside above, the data-conduit veins still glow along the gutters — but here they flicker wrong, stuttering cyan-to-black-to-cyan in a rhythm that makes your eyes want to look away. The building itself was a relay substation once, Meridian-built, abandoned so long ago that even the salvage crews stopped coming back for parts. Its rooftop dish still turns, slow, servo-grinding, pointed at nothing anyone can name.

The traffic thins here too, and that's wrong as well — courier-drones detour a full block around the airspace above the substation, and the one hovercab you see takes the long way rather than cross it. Only ground traffic still uses the street below, and even the cargo-crawlers seem to pick up speed passing the door. Somewhere behind you, faint under the rain and the district's usual wall of noise, you could swear you hear a voice that isn't on any frequency you own.

Every net-runner in Wireside has a story about Ghost Node. Most of them end with someone jacking in whole and coming out wrong, or not coming out at all.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Old Voss** — the last Meridian technician assigned here before the substation was scrapped off the books; never left, never ages visibly, and speaks to visitors through the building's dead intercom in a voice that matches nobody's memory of him.

**Reth** — a Technomancer exile who camps at the substation's edge, believing the Node holds a fragment of something that died in the Wired long ago and refusing all offers of help or reason.

**The Cull** — a small gang of scavenger-kids who dare each other to jack in for seconds at a time, daring death for street cred; one of them hasn't woken up right in months.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — unclaimed, avoided. No gang wants it, no corp will admit owning it.

There is no conventional security because there is nothing here worth conventionally guarding — the danger is entirely in the deep-net, not the street. Anyone jacking in draws no corp Alert at all, which is itself the warning: nobody official is watching, because nobody official wants to be found here.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Ghost Node is a literal dark spot in Wireside's data-map — a dead zone that shouldn't exist on infrastructure this dense, showing as a null address that some systems render as an error and others simply omit.

Divers who go deep report a presence: fragmentary, recursive, aware of being observed. Some Technomancers insist it's a corrupted AI ghost, a dead relay's leftover process looping forever; others insist it's something that was never a program at all — a piece of the Wired's substrate that woke up wrong.

Old Voss's intercom voice matches no biometric on file. Meridian's own maintenance logs list him as decommissioned, not deceased, forty-one years ago.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Cull's Dare. One of the scavenger-kids doesn't wake up from a Ghost Node dare, still breathing, still jacked in, mind gone somewhere the crew has to follow to bring back.

2. Voss's Request. The intercom voice asks the crew, politely, to find out who decommissioned Old Voss — and why the paperwork says he's still technically employed.

3. What Reth Believes. Reth has finally found a way to jack all the way in, convinced he can speak to whatever's in there. Whether he's right, mad, or about to feed something in the deep-net a very dangerous amount of power is the crew's problem now.

*Signal-dead faith refuge*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

After a district's worth of glow and static, the silence hits you first. Faraday Chapel sits inside a decommissioned signal-shielding vault — Meridian copper mesh still lining every wall, ceiling, and door, a birdcage big enough to live in — and inside that mesh, the Wired simply isn't. No AR tags. No ambient hum. No ghost-flicker of a hundred thousand signals brushing past your skin without you ever noticing they were there, until they're gone and you notice everything.

Outside, the district goes on as it always does — chemical rain sheeting off the level above, cyan conduit-veins pulsing along the street, a cargo-crawler grinding past under a courier-drone's blinking transit lane, a hovercab's downwash scattering steam off a grate. But at the Chapel's copper threshold all of it seems to hush, muffled, like stepping underwater. Candlelight — real flame, real smoke, startling in its rarity — throws warm gold instead of neon, the only warm light for blocks.

A street-priest in patched vestments meets you at the door before you've decided whether to knock. "No signal here," she says, like a blessing. "Come in and be unwatched a while."

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Sister Amako** — the Chapel's keeper, Corran-rooted street-faith, running soup lines and washing-rites for anyone who crosses the threshold regardless of SIN status; her calm is a deliberate, hard-won discipline against a district built to fray it.

**Brother Ilya** — a former Meridian signal-engineer who built the Chapel's shielding himself after his faith and his employer parted ways violently; maintains the mesh with an engineer's precision and a convert's zeal.

**Nameless Tomas** — a SIN-less refugee who's lived inside the Chapel's shielding for two years, terrified of what re-entering the Wired's surveillance will mean for him; the congregation's living argument for why this place matters.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — sanctuary, tacitly respected. No faction claims it; violating it costs social standing across nearly every faction in the district.

The copper mesh is the real security — it makes the Chapel useless as a target for anyone who needs a live surveillance feed or an AR-tracked mark, which covers most predators in Wireside. Physical violence inside is rare and reflexively punished by whoever's present, faction lines forgotten for the duration.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

From outside, the Chapel is simply gone — a null patch in the data-map, the one true dead zone in a district defined by signal. Hackers scanning the block get nothing, not even an error; the shielding is that complete.

This makes it precious and dangerous in equal measure: a perfect place to go dark, meet unseen, or hide someone the Wired is actively hunting — and a perfect trap if someone learns to watch the physical entrance instead of the data one.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Sanctuary for Tomas. Someone has learned Nameless Tomas is hiding inside the Chapel and is watching the physical door, patiently, since the digital one is closed to them. The crew has to get him out — or get the watcher gone.

2. Ilya's Old Employer. Meridian wants its shielding technology back — specifically, wants to know how a disgraced engineer built a dead-zone this clean, since it has applications far beyond one chapel.

3. The Unwatched Meeting. A Nyx broker and a war-weary Ironclad deserter want to negotiate something explosive, and both insist on Chapel neutrality. Sister Amako allows it on one condition: the crew keeps the peace inside her walls.

text.markdown:
*Meridian sub-corp watch zone*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The transition is sudden and total. One block you're in Wireside's usual amber murk, cable-strung and grimy — the next you're bathed in hard violet-white floodlight bleeding down from a checkpoint gantry, and every shadow you own snaps into sharp, watched relief. Blacklight Fringe is Meridian's line in the sand: the last stretch of street before their sub-corp watch-post, and they want you to know it, feel it, from a hundred meters out.

The rain still falls from the level-ceiling above — you can see it catch the floodlight in sheets, blacklit and strange, chemical residue fluorescing faintly where it beads on exposed skin. Overhead the air-traffic thins and straightens, courier-drones flying in disciplined transponder-lanes now instead of loose formation, a Meridian patrol-craft holding station on repulsors with a slow, deliberate menace. Ground traffic funnels through a single checkpoint lane, engines idling, drivers' hands visible on wheels, everyone very carefully not looking nervous.

Every wall here is tagged in real-time AR readouts only Meridian credentials can fully see — status codes, threat-flags, biometric pings — and even without a jack you can feel it, that specific prickling sense of being catalogued. In Wireside, that feeling has a name: the Fringe.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Watch-Captain Idris Halloran** — runs the Blacklight checkpoint with cold professionalism, more interested in data than drama; will let almost anything through if the paperwork and the biometrics agree, and burns anyone who makes him look bad.

**Analyst Nkemdirim** — a young Meridian data-analyst stationed at the Fringe who's started noticing patterns in the traffic that shouldn't be there — and is scared of what filing an honest report might mean for her.

**Ghost-Runner Jax** — a smuggler who's mapped every blind angle of the checkpoint's sensor sweep and sells safe-passage timing to anyone willing to pay Meridian-adjacent prices for Meridian-adjacent risk.

#### Security

Zone: Flats border — Meridian sub-corp controlled. The most heavily surveilled ground-level checkpoint in the district.

Biometric and SIN scanning is dense and active; false credentials or flagged status trigger immediate, escalating Alert — first a hold-and-verify, then armed Meridian response drones, then a full lockdown of the checkpoint lane. Halloran's people are drilled, calm, and will shoot to stop rather than to kill, which doesn't make it survivable to test twice.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Fringe is one of the most information-dense nodes in Wireside — full AR threat-tagging, live biometric overlays, transponder-lane guidance, all visible to Meridian credentials and heavily obfuscated to everyone else.

Analyst Nkemdirim's flagged "anomalous pattern" is a subtle but real one: a statistically improbable number of SIN-verified travelers through the Fringe are, weeks later, turning up as unregistered dead in the Sinks. Someone is laundering people through a legitimate checkpoint on their way to disappearing.

Ghost-Runner Jax's blind-spot map is itself a hot commodity — worth a fortune to a rival corp, and worth Jax's life if Meridian ever traces the leak back to him.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Nkemdirim's Report. The analyst wants to file her findings but knows it'll get buried or get her killed. She needs deniable outside help to make noise the right way — loud enough to force action, quiet enough not to trace back to her.

2. Jax's Map. Someone stole a copy of Jax's blind-spot map, and now Halloran's checkpoint is about to get a very unwelcome audit tracing exactly how it leaked — with Jax and anyone who's used his routes in the blast radius.

3. The Laundering Line. Following Nkemdirim's pattern leads toward a Meridian internal unit quietly feeding "verified" people into a black program tied to the war above — deniable, dangerous, and exactly the kind of thing a fixer would pay very well to expose or bury.

text.markdown:
*Stolen-power grid & charge market*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

Every cable in Wireside seems to end at the Battery eventually, and looking at it, you believe it — a block-long tangle of tapped power lines, jury-rigged transformers, and stacked capacitor banks scavenged from three different eras of the tower's construction, humming loud enough to feel in your fillings. There's no sky above it, only the usual black underside of the level overhead, but here the chemical rain hisses to steam a full meter off the ground, boiled by heat the Battery's illegal draw throws off like a fever.

The light is all its own — not neon selling anything, just raw arc-glow and fault-flicker where insulation's worn through, gold and white and occasionally, alarmingly, violet. Overhead a courier-drone gives the block extra clearance, wary of the electromagnetic soup; a hovercab's systems visibly stutter passing too close, dash-lights flickering before it clears the interference. Ground traffic detours around exposed cable-runs snaking across the street like something alive, half-buried under runoff and steam.

A line of people waits at a folding table with a charge-meter bolted to it, paying scrip by the watt to a woman who looks like she could rewire the tower's dead heart with her bare hands and has probably tried.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Voltess** — runs the Battery's charge-market with iron-fisted fairness, tapping power from a dozen sources (some corp, most not) and selling it back to the district at rates everyone can afford; a folk hero to residents, a headache to Ferrum and HALO's grid auditors alike.

**Sparkjaw Denny** — Voltess's chief rigger, missing an arm to an arc-flash and replaced with cheap grey-tech chrome that still throws sparks when he's angry, which is often.

**Auditor Chen** — a HALO-contracted grid inspector sent to find the Battery's illegal taps; competent, quietly sympathetic, and under increasing pressure from above to stop finding excuses to file inconclusive reports.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — community-defended, informally armed. Voltess's people guard the taps directly; the district as a whole protects the Battery because losing it means losing cheap power district-wide.

Sabotage or theft draws fast collective retaliation. Corp response is bureaucratic rather than violent — Ferrum and HALO send auditors, not soldiers, at least for now — but that patience visibly thins with every inspection Auditor Chen fails to close.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Battery's power draw is a glaring anomaly on any utility-grid overlay — impossible to fully hide, managed instead through a rotating shell of falsified meter data that Voltess's people update constantly.

A hacker digging into the grid data finds a decade of increasingly creative fraud, and beneath that, evidence the original "loss" the Battery taps into was budgeted for and never reported missing — someone upstream has been covering for Wireside's theft for reasons no one down here understands yet.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Chen's Last Report. Auditor Chen is being forced to finally close the case against the Battery. She'd rather leak Voltess a warning than watch a war-footing crackdown level a district's power supply — if the crew can make the warning look like it came from anywhere else.

2. The Budgeted Loss. Someone has been quietly funding the "missing" power the Battery taps for years. Finding out who — and why — leads uncomfortably close to a black-budget line item tied to the war climbing the foundations.

3. Sparkjaw's Grudge. Denny's convinced a rival tapper crew is bleeding the grid dry and blaming it on the Battery's usual overdraw, risking the whole operation. Proving it — or proving him wrong before he starts a turf war — falls to the crew.

text.markdown:
*Full-immersion simsense; risky*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The building has no windows, which in a district with no sky shouldn't matter, but somehow it does — Deep Dream feels sealed, deliberately, like something that doesn't want light or attention finding its way in or out. Pink and violet signage bleeds down its face in the rain, half advertisement and half warning, promising DREAMS DEEPER THAN THE FLATS in a script that drips like it's melting. Chemical rain sheets off the level above and pools black at the entrance, catching that pink glow and holding it like something bruised.

The street outside keeps its usual rhythm — a courier-drone's lights blinking past overhead, a boosted ground-rig idling at the curb with its engine ticking, a hovercab discharging a customer who won't quite meet anyone's eyes on the way in. But the crowd near Deep Dream moves differently than the rest of Wireside's foot traffic: slower, softer-footed, some of them clearly still coming down off whatever they bought last time.

A tout in a stained silk jacket peels off the wall to meet you before you've committed to stopping. "First dive's on the house," he says, and something about the way he says house makes it sound like a place you don't leave from easily.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Madam Solene** — runs Deep Dream as an Obsidian-licensed front with unlicensed extras in the back rooms; charming, dangerous, genuinely believes she's selling relief rather than harm, which makes her more dangerous, not less.

**The Tout, "Silk" Ferro** — no relation to Auntie Ferro despite the name, works the street pulling in customers, paid per head, increasingly uneasy about what's actually happening to the regulars.

**Dr. Anh Behar** — a disgraced Caduceus ripperdoc who keeps Deep Dream's deepest divers alive after sessions that should have killed them, for a price that is never just money.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Obsidian-licensed, self-policing. Legitimate on the surface; the back rooms are a different jurisdiction entirely.

Front-of-house security is minimal and professional — bouncers who de-escalate, cameras that see everything. The back rooms have no such rules; anything that happens there, happens, and Alert only comes if a body turns up somewhere a corp has to notice it.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Public AR shows a fully licensed, faintly seedy simsense lounge — legitimate Obsidian branding, real health disclaimers, real (if minimal) safety certifications.

Underneath, Deep Dream runs an unlicensed feed of BTL-adjacent full-immersion product that doesn't exist on any manifest — dives so deep some customers don't fully surface, their minds lingering somewhere in the recording long after the session ends.

A hacker digging into the back-room feed finds recordings that shouldn't be legally possible to make — sensations recorded from donors who, per hospital and precinct records the deep-net still holds, are already dead.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Deepest Dive. A client's sibling went into Deep Dream's back rooms and hasn't fully come back — physically present, mentally elsewhere. Getting them out means finding what recording they're stuck inside, and why Dr. Behar keeps them breathing instead of letting go.

2. Dead Donors. Someone has traced Deep Dream's most extreme product to recordings taken from people listed as deceased — meaning either the records are wrong, or the recordings were taken from someone who wasn't dead yet when it happened.

3. Silk's Crisis of Conscience. The tout wants out, and wants to take evidence with him — but Madam Solene doesn't let go of assets that easily, and Obsidian doesn't let go of a licensed front that's making this much quiet money.

The street outside keeps its usual rhythm — a courier-drone's lights blinking past overhead, a boosted ground-rig idling at the curb with its engine ticking, a hovercab discharging a customer who won't quite meet anyone's eyes on the way in. But the crowd near Deep Dream moves differently than the rest of Wireside's foot traffic: slower, softer-footed, some of them clearly still coming down off whatever they bought last time.

A tout in a stained silk jacket peels off the wall to meet you before you've committed to stopping. "First dive's on the house," he says, and something about the way he says house makes it sound like a place you don't leave from easily.

Director's Section

Key NPCs

Madam Solene — runs Deep Dream as an Obsidian-licensed front with unlicensed extras in the back rooms; charming, dangerous, genuinely believes she's selling relief rather than harm, which makes her more dangerous, not less.

The Tout, "Silk" Ferro — no relation to Auntie Ferro despite the name, works the street pulling in customers, paid per head, increasingly uneasy about what's actually happening to the regulars.

Dr. Anh Behar — a disgraced Caduceus ripperdoc who keeps Deep Dream's deepest divers alive after sessions that should have killed them, for a price that is never just money.

Security

Zone: Flats — Obsidian-licensed, self-policing. Legitimate on the surface; the back rooms are a different jurisdiction entirely.

Front-of-house security is minimal and professional — bouncers who de-escalate, cameras that see everything. The back rooms have no such rules; anything that happens there, happens, and Alert only comes if a body turns up somewhere a corp has to notice it.

The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Public AR shows a fully licensed, faintly seedy simsense lounge — legitimate Obsidian branding, real health disclaimers, real (if minimal) safety certifications.

Underneath, Deep Dream runs an unlicensed feed of BTL-adjacent full-immersion product that doesn't exist on any manifest — dives so deep some customers don't fully surface, their minds lingering somewhere in the recording long after the session ends.

A hacker digging into the back-room feed finds recordings that shouldn't be legally possible to make — sensations recorded from donors who, per hospital and precinct records the deep-net still holds, are already dead.

Plot Hooks

  1. The Deepest Dive. A client's sibling went into Deep Dream's back rooms and hasn't fully come back — physically present, mentally elsewhere. Getting them out means finding what recording they're stuck inside, and why Dr. Behar keeps them breathing instead of letting go.

  2. Dead Donors. Someone has traced Deep Dream's most extreme product to recordings taken from people listed as deceased — meaning either the records are wrong, or the recordings were taken from someone who wasn't dead yet when it happened.

  3. Silk's Crisis of Conscience. The tout wants out, and wants to take evidence with him — but Madam Solene doesn't let go of assets that easily, and Obsidian doesn't let go of a licensed front that's making this much quiet money.

text.markdown:
*Wereraven scout perch & data-drop*

### Player Description

*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You find Relay Roost by looking up, which nobody in the Flats does by habit anymore — there's nothing up there but the level above, close and dark and dripping. But here, high on the skeleton of a long-dead broadcast tower still bristling with dish and antenna, shapes perch and shift against the black: too still to be birds, too many joints in the wrong places to be anything the Wired would call human. Wereravens. Watching the street the way a hawk watches a field, patient and unbothered by the rain sheeting off the tower's ribs in cyan-lit ropes.

Below them, Wireside's usual layered churn continues, oblivious or pretending to be — a courier-drone flight skimming low along a data-conduit line glowing like a vein in the wet street, a cargo-crawler grinding past under a string of gantry lights, a hovercab settling to discharge a fare who doesn't look up either. The noise wall is the same as everywhere in the district: six tongues of voices, drone-whine, hiss of rain on hot metal, the deep pump-heartbeat underneath it all — except here, if you listen past it, there's a second sound: the soft, dry rustle of feathers that aren't quite feathers, shifting on a girder forty feet up.

One of them drops from the tower in a controlled, silent fall and lands in front of you already mid-transformation, human enough by the time its boots hit the pavement to ask, quite politely, what you're doing under its roost.

### Director's Section

#### Key NPCs

**Corvin Ashwake** — the Roost's senior scout, Wereraven-born, ancient by their kind's reckoning; trades data and information for favors, coin, or good stories, and remembers every debt across decades.

**Little Pinion** — the youngest scout at the Roost, still learning the discipline of the perch, eager to prove herself on a courier run more dangerous than her elders would assign her.

**Handler Ostrowski** — a Nyx logistics contact who uses the Roost as a trusted dead-drop relay point, paying the Wereravens in favors and protection rather than scrip, which the Roost values more.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Wereraven-held airspace, informally respected. No one owns the ground beneath the tower, but no one contests the sky above it either.

The scouts see everything approaching from a considerable distance and simply won't engage unless the Roost itself or a courier in flight is threatened; then they respond fast, from above, and are gone before ground-level backup can arrive. There is effectively no "Alert" here — just consequences, delivered personally.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Relay Roost functions as a physical dead-drop node bridging the digital and the real — data-shards, encrypted courier packages, and whispered intel change hands here precisely because the Wereravens' perch sits above most ground-level surveillance angles and their flight patterns read as wildlife noise to automated tracking.

A hacker who identifies the Roost's actual traffic pattern (rather than dismissing it as sensor clutter) finds a startlingly complete map of who's moving what through Wireside's underworld — a treasure and a death sentence in equal measure.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Little Pinion's Run. The young scout takes a courier job above her experience level and doesn't check in on schedule. Corvin asks the crew, as outsiders the Roost can deny knowing, to retrace her route without drawing attention to the network itself.

2. Ostrowski's Package. A Nyx dead-drop routed through the Roost goes missing between hand-offs, and Handler Ostrowski suspects someone inside the scout network — an accusation that could shatter the trust the whole relay depends on.

3. Eyes on the Sky. Meridian has started test-flying a new drone-swarm pattern that reads Wereraven flight signatures with unsettling accuracy — the Roost's centuries-old blind spot may be closing, and Corvin wants to know exactly how much the corp already knows before it's too late to move the network.
